summary: Discusses interoperability and security problems of oversized IPv6 header chains that spill past the first fragment, and updates RFC 2460 to require the first fragment to contain the entire chain. This is a security and interoperability fix to the original IPv6 specification.

plainLanguage.summary: All the labels must fit on the first page, so the guards can read them.

questions: what is an ipv6 header chain
why must the first fragment contain all ipv6 headers
subtitle: IPv6 packets must keep their whole header chain in the first fragment, so firewalls can do their job.

tldr.problem: IPv6 allows arbitrarily long chains of extension headers, so after fragmentation the first fragment may not contain the upper-layer header, and stateless firewalls cannot enforce their policy.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7112 updates RFC 2460 so that a host that fragments a datagram MUST put the entire IPv6 Header Chain in the First Fragment, and defines an ICMPv6 Parameter Problem code for discards.
tldr.outcome: Fragmented packets that evade stateless filtering are forbidden, and header chains can no longer exceed the Path MTU. Hosts that do not discover the Path MTU must keep the chain within 1280 bytes.

today: RFC 7112 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 2460, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its rule is that the First Fragment must contain the entire IPv6 Header Chain.

sections.title: The Header Chain Problem
sections.content:
IPv6 carries optional internet-layer information in Extension Headers, placed between the IPv6 header and the Upper-Layer Header. Together these form the IPv6 Header Chain. IPv4 had a fixed maximum length for all its options, but IPv6 has no equivalent limit. If the chain is unusually long and the packet is fragmented, or the fragments are very small, the chain can spill across several fragments.

This document sets an overall limit by updating RFC 2460 so that the First Fragment of a fragmented datagram must contain the entire chain. The rule does not forbid large payloads. It only requires that every header from the IPv6 base header up to the Upper-Layer Header, such as TCP, be in the First Fragment.
sections.plainLanguage: A packet has a stack of labels on the front. The rule says that when a packet is cut into pieces, all of the labels must be on the first piece.

sections.title: Key Terms
sections.content:
A First Fragment is an IPv6 fragment with Fragment Offset equal to 0. The IPv6 Header Chain holds an initial IPv6 header, zero or more Extension Headers, and optionally a single Upper-Layer Header. An Upper-Layer Header ends the chain; if there is none, the "No Next Header" value (Next Header = 59) ends it.

A header joins the chain only if the previous header's Next Header field points to it. Two cases end the chain early: a second IPv6 header (as when IPv6 is tunneled over IPv6) and an Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) header are both treated as the Upper-Layer Header. The upper-layer payload, such as TCP data, is not part of the chain.
sections.plainLanguage: The header chain is the whole row of labels from the first one down to the one that says what is inside, like TCP. The stuff inside the box does not count as a label.

sections.title: Why Firewalls Need It
sections.content:
Many forwarding devices run stateless firewalls, which judge each packet on its own and may need to read both IPv6 and upper-layer headers. Suppose a firewall drops everything except traffic to one TCP port on one IPv6 address. If a fragmented packet aimed at another port has its whole chain in the First Fragment, the firewall drops that fragment and lets the rest pass. The packet can never be reassembled, so the policy holds.

If the chain spans several fragments, the First Fragment lacks the information the firewall needs. It must either forward or discard blindly, and either way it may fail to enforce its policy.
sections.plainLanguage: A guard checks the first page for the destination. If the destination is not on the first page, the guard has to guess, and might let in a letter that should have been stopped.

sections.title: The Updated Rule
sections.content:
When a host fragments an IPv6 datagram, it MUST include the entire Header Chain in the First Fragment. A host that receives a non-compliant First Fragment SHOULD discard the packet and SHOULD send an ICMPv6 error to the source, subject to the rules of RFC 4443. For backwards compatibility, implementations MAY offer a setting to accept such fragments.

An intermediate system such as a router or firewall MAY discard such a packet and MAY send the ICMPv6 error. Systems with this capability SHOULD let the operator enable or disable dropping. Any ICMPv6 error sent MUST be Type 4 (Parameter Problem) with Code 3, "First Fragment has incomplete IPv6 Header Chain", and the Pointer field MUST be zero.

One consequence is that a chain cannot be longer than the Path MTU to its destination. Hosts discover this using RFC 1981 or RFC 4821. Hosts that do not discover the Path MTU MUST limit the chain to 1280 bytes, which is the IPv6 minimum MTU.
sections.plainLanguage: Senders must put all the labels on page one. Receivers can send back a note saying the labels were missing. If the sender does not know how big the envelope can be, it keeps the labels small enough for the smallest envelope.

sections.title: Security and IANA Notes
sections.content:
The RFC says it raises no new security exposures. Hiding the upper-layer header behind fragmentation can evade stateless packet filtering, and by forbidding such packets the update removes that vulnerability. It also warns that deploying source address forgery prevention filters ( RFC 2827, RFC 3704) reduces the chance that an attacker uses the new ICMPv6 errors for a reflection attack with a forged victim address.

A firewall that does stateless deep packet inspection of application payload might still be unable to process fragmented packets correctly, even when the header chain is not fragmented. IANA added Code 3, "IPv6 First Fragment has incomplete IPv6 Header Chain", to the Type 4 Parameter Problem entries of the ICMPv6 Parameters registry.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the labels are always on the first page, a sneaky sender cannot hide them on later pages to fool the guard.

viz.caption: WHO MUST, SHOULD OR MAY DO WHAT

items.title: Fragmenting host
items.text: MUST put the entire Header Chain in the First Fragment.

items.title: Receiving host
items.text: SHOULD discard a bad First Fragment and SHOULD send an ICMPv6 error.

items.title: Router or firewall
items.text: MAY discard it and MAY send the error; SHOULD allow this to be configured.

items.title: ICMPv6 error
items.text: Type 4, Code 3, with the Pointer field set to zero.
